keyVerseText: Even the very dust of your city, which cleaveth on us, we do wipe off against you: notwithstanding be ye sure of this, that the kingdom of God is come nigh unto you.
rootMeaning: The Greek verb κολλάω (kolláō) originates from the noun κόλλα (kólla), meaning 'glue.' This etymology highlights the fundamental idea of sticking or cementing together, which conveys a strong sense of adhesion or joining. Unlike the more general English terms 'join' or 'cleave,' the root sense emphasizes a bond that is firm and enduring, much like glue that permanently unites separate parts.
usageInScripture: Across its ten occurrences, κολλάω consistently conveys the action of joining or cleaving, whether it be persons joining themselves to others or things sticking together. The top translations such as 'cleaveth,' 'join himself,' and 'to keep company' reflect this range from physical adhesion to relational attachment. This consistency reveals the word's flexibility in describing both literal and figurative forms of union, from the physical act of gluing to the spiritual or social act of close association.
theologicalSignificance: Understanding κολλάω enriches our grasp of biblical unity and relational closeness within the Christian faith. The idea of cleaving or joining firmly echoes the biblical call to believers to be united with Christ and with one another in a bond that cannot be easily broken. This verb underscores the permanence and intentionality of spiritual fellowship and covenant relationship, reminding us that faith is not a casual association but a committed, adhesive union with God and His people. Such a bond reflects the transformative power of the gospel, which joins believers not only to God but also into a new community.
keyVerseReflection: In Luke 10:11, the phrase 'Even the very dust of your city, which cleaveth on us' uses κολλάω to describe dust that sticks firmly to the disciples, symbolizing the close, unavoidable contact with the city's rejection. The word's meaning of strong adhesion emphasizes the tangible evidence of rejection that the disciples carry, yet it also contrasts with the assured nearness of the kingdom of God. This highlights how, despite external opposition, the spiritual union and mission of God's kingdom remain steadfast and present.
